title: Checkpoint: The Chemistry of Life
objective: After this level you can explain how chemistry powers living things.
summary: Plants respire too: they have mitochondria as well as chloroplasts. Follow one carbon atom from the air into a leaf, a potato, your mouth, your cells and back out on your breath.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale: plants breathe out carbon dioxide too.
cards.body: Plants make sugar, you burn it. A neat division of labor? Not quite. Then follow one carbon atom through the whole chapter.

cards.headline: Plants respire too
cards.body: You might think plants only photosynthesize. Plant cells have mitochondria as well as chloroplasts. The chloroplasts make sugar from light; the mitochondria then burn some of that sugar in cellular respiration, making ATP, just as yours do. A plant is both the chef and a diner at its own restaurant.

cards.headline: One carbon atom's round trip
cards.body: Start with a carbon atom in the air's carbon dioxide. A potato leaf pulls it in and, by photosynthesis, builds it into glucose, then stores it in the tuber as starch. You eat the potato; amylase starts breaking the starch into sugar. Your cells respire the glucose in their mitochondria, and the carbon rides out on your breath as carbon dioxide, ready for the next leaf.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete
learned: How plants build sugar from air, water and light, and how your cells release its energy step by step.
Why shape is everything for proteins and enzymes, and how heat can wreck it for good.
Why you can digest starch but not cellulose, and why butter is solid while olive oil pours.
What makes something a poison: the dose, not the substance alone.

questions.prompt: Chemistry of life: which energy-handling compartments does a plant cell contain?

options.label: Neither; plants get energy from soil
options.rationale: Plants make sugar from light and burn it in mitochondria.

questions.explanation: Plant cells have chloroplasts for photosynthesis and mitochondria for cellular respiration.

questions.prompt: A plant makes its own sugar. Why does it still need cellular respiration?

options.label: To make more carbon dioxide for photosynthesis
options.rationale: That's a side effect, not the purpose.

options.label: It doesn't; only animals respire
options.rationale: Plant cells have mitochondria and respire too.

options.label: To turn sugar back into soil
options.rationale: Respiration makes carbon dioxide and water, not soil.

options.label: To release the sugar's energy as ATP

questions.explanation: Making sugar stores energy; respiration in the plant's mitochondria releases it as ATP the cells can use.

questions.prompt: Chemistry of life recap: which element makes up the largest share of your body's mass?

options.label: Carbon
options.rationale: Carbon is second, at about 18 percent.

options.label: Hydrogen
options.rationale: Hydrogen leads by number of atoms, not by mass.

questions.explanation: By mass you're about 65 percent oxygen, 18 percent carbon, 10 percent hydrogen and 3 percent nitrogen.

questions.prompt: Chemistry of life recap: on the carbon atom's round trip, which process moves it from the air into a leaf's glucose?

options.label: Cellular respiration
options.rationale: Respiration sends carbon back into the air.

options.label: Denaturation
options.rationale: That's a protein losing its shape.

options.label: Digestion by amylase
options.rationale: Amylase works later, in your mouth.

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis turns carbon dioxide and water, with light, into glucose and oxygen.

questions.prompt: Chemistry of life recap: by Paracelsus's principle, can a glass of ordinary water ever be poisonous?

options.label: No, water is never harmful
options.rationale: Even water is poisonous if far too much is taken in.

options.label: Yes, if far too much is taken in
Only if it is cold
options.rationale: Temperature isn't the deciding factor; amount is.

options.label: Only if it is distilled
options.rationale: Pure or not, the dose is what matters.

questions.explanation: The dose makes the poison: even a substance as harmless as water is poisonous in a large enough amount.
